acknowledgment: Constructive, non-harming shepherding: preserve evidence, distinguish allegations from findings, and avoid ancestry-based blame or invented motives.
scope: Four selected cases within 1776–1860, not an exhaustive account of the period or a ranking of all influence.

findings.title: Plantation and shipping interests in slave-importation bargaining
findings.measurement: No paid or promised political transfer quantified
findings.mechanism: Madison records General Charles Cotesworth Pinckney defending slave imports through plantation output, shipping, consumption and revenue, and warning of lost South Carolina assent. Rutledge also tied consent to protecting imports. [E01]
findings.policy_instrument: Constitution Article I section 9; Article V
findings.outcome: Congress could not prohibit covered importations before 1808. The text allowed a duty up to $10 per person; that ceiling is neither a verified collection nor a bribe. [E02]
findings.evidence_strength: Direct recorded economic-interest argument and enacted constitutional protection; no check-to-vote trace.
findings.counterevidence: Mason opposed the trade; Sherman prioritized forming the Union despite disapproval. Economic incentives and constitutional bargaining were interwoven. [E01]

lineage.documented: The debate expressly connects enslaved labor, rice-region demand and carrying trade to political bargaining. [E01]
lineage.actor_role: Pinckney and Rutledge: South Carolina convention delegates.
lineage.continuity_boundary: Protection was time-limited. These records identify historical interests, not modern descendants' liability, childhood causes or a continuous corporate ownership chain.

findings.title: Creditor claims and federal assumption of state war debts
findings.payer: United States, through statutory debt funding
findings.measurement: Nominal statutory subscription ceiling, not cash paid
findings.payment_status: Authorization; actual subscriptions and later payments not audited here.
findings.mechanism: Hamilton opposed reducing purchasers' claims to their acquisition cost, arguing that transferable claims, contracts and borrowing terms supported public credit. Congress authorized exchange of qualifying state war-debt certificates for federal obligations. [E03,E04]
findings.outcome: Federal funding terms protected eligible certificate holders and assumed defined state liabilities. The $21.5 million ceiling was payable through certificates, not a $21.5 million cash lobbying fund. [E04]
findings.evidence_strength: Strong fiscal distribution and creditor-policy connection; paid lobbying or a purchased vote not established.
findings.counterevidence: Hamilton presents the alternative of favoring original holders who sold cheaply, and argues against it on contract and public-credit grounds. [E03]

lineage.documented: Revolutionary war financing generated claims traded between original holders and purchasers; the report distinguishes foreign contractual debt from domestic restructuring. [E03]
lineage.continuity_boundary: Public-credit institutions connect finance and policy; no specific merchant/plantation fortune or modern successor ownership is traced here.

findings.title: Yazoo land interests, legislative corruption and purchaser protection
findings.recipient: Georgia treasury; legislators allegedly promised land interests
findings.measurement: Georgia Company statutory purchase terms: $50,000 before grant plus $200,000 due November 1, 1795
findings.payment_status: Terms recited in litigation; no independent cash receipt audit. Bribe amount remains null.
findings.mechanism: The complaint alleged Gunn, M'Allister and Walker promised legislators land shares for favorable votes. Georgia's repeal preamble separately declared corruption and participating legislators' purchase interests. [E05,E06]
findings.policy_instrument: Georgia sale act of January 7, 1795; repeal of February 13, 1796; Fletcher v. Peck (1810)
findings.outcome: Repeal attacked the grants. The Court protected an innocent subsequent purchaser's vested rights; it did not adjudicate each alleged bribe. [E06]
findings.evidence_strength: Legislative corruption finding plus specific judicially recorded allegations; neither an audited bribe total nor a criminal verdict.
findings.counterevidence: Peck disputed the promises and asserted lack of notice. Judicial reasoning protected purchasers rather than endorsing corruption. [E06]

lineage.documented: Land-company ownership incentives reached legislative allocation of territory. The repeal contrasted $500,000 accepted consideration with an $800,000 rejected offer. [E05]
lineage.actor_role: Named purchasers, Georgia legislators, governor and later courts.
lineage.continuity_boundary: Speculation-to-law mechanism established at this scope; specific plantation profits, later heirs and current beneficiaries not traced.

findings.title: Bank publicity spending and failed federal recharter
findings.payer: Second Bank of the United States
findings.recipient: Printers/publication vendors; complete named payees unavailable in selected account
findings.measurement: Approximate expenditure reported by Jackson for 1831–1832, not an independently audited exact total
findings.payment_status: Presidential report cites board authorization, partial vouchers and additional orders without vouchers. [E07]
findings.mechanism: Bank-funded circulation of favorable articles, congressional reports and speeches aimed at public opinion and charter renewal; the March 1831 resolution described public information about the bank. [E07]
findings.policy_instrument: Recharter bill veto; executive deposit-removal policy statement
findings.outcome: Jackson vetoed the bill on July 10, 1832. Its proposed $3 million bonus/$200,000 annual payment was not enacted by that bill. [E08]
findings.evidence_strength: Direct reported institutional advocacy spending; recipient-level accounting and vote causation incomplete.
findings.counterevidence: Spending did not secure the charter. Jackson's adverse account also identifies independent charter-expiry and administrative reasons for deposit removal. [E07,E08]

lineage.documented: A chartered bank used institutional resources to defend privileges; the veto discusses benefits to domestic and foreign stockholders. [E08]
lineage.continuity_boundary: Institutional publicity is a comparable mechanism, not proof that a modern bank inherits this entity's acts or that Jackson's accusation is neutral accounting.

notes: All amounts are historical nominal units. No inflation adjustment, cross-case sum or inferred amount per vote is supplied.
These cases distinguish public debt obligations, economic-interest bargaining, alleged private inducements and corporate publicity. They are not four equally established bribery cases.
Foreign or public war financing is not classified as private lobbying; the 1790 case concerns the allocation and funding of debt claims.
Slavery was human exploitation, not merely a neutral commodity input. Historical actors' financial descriptions are reported as evidence of their arguments.
No motive is inferred from childhood, ancestry, race or descendants. Contemporary continuity requires separate documented ownership, legal, organizational or policy links.
The period label is 1776–1860; selected cases cluster in 1787–1833 and do not claim comprehensive coverage of the entire interval.
No fresh outreach, publication, local research compute job or historical test suite was run.
